meta.regime: The energy shock that pushed seven of eight central banks the same way has started to unwind, and for the first time in two weeks the barrel and the curve are pointing in opposite directions: Iranian and US negotiators held side talks at the UN on a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and WTI fell 2.33% to 92.410 with Brent down 2.14% to 104.320, yet almost none of the hawkish repricing came back out. The one place it hardened is the one that matters on Monday - TradingEconomics has abandoned its 4.35% hold call and now carries 4.60% for the RBA, matching a market that prices 92-94% - so the board splits into currencies whose hawkishness survives cheaper crude and currencies whose hawkishness was only ever the crude.
meta.nextBigEvent: The RBA on Monday September 29 at 04:30Z, and the disagreement this page has tracked for a week is gone: TradingEconomics now carries both consensus and its own forecast at 4.60%, against 4.35% previous, which lines the canonical source up with 92-94% market pricing and all four major Australian banks. A hike makes Australia the highest policy rate of the majors at 60bp above the Fed's upper bound and 210bp above the ECB, which is why the risk in AUD is no longer direction but sell-the-fact. After that: Tokyo CPI on October 1, FOMC minutes October 7, then the October 28-30 cluster of the Fed, Bank of Canada, RBNZ and the UK Budget on the 28th, the ECB on the 29th and the Bank of Japan on the 30th, eight days before a November 5 BoE meeting Bailey has now opened.

dailyRead: Friday resolved two of the three questions this page has been carrying, and it resolved them in opposite directions. The first was geopolitical. Crude fell hard - WTI 92.410 and Brent 104.320, down 2.33% and 2.14%, with gasoline down 4.80% - after Iranian and US negotiators held side talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly about a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the same channel that produced the collapsed June 17 memorandum. That matters far beyond energy, because the hawkish repricing of the last fortnight was built on one input. Bailey's own hawkishness was explicitly conditioned on it: he said Thursday it would 'get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices'. Lombardelli and Breeden made the same conditional argument. RBNZ Governor Breman warned near-term inflation could overshoot if higher crude persists. If Brent keeps falling, those are the arguments that weaken first, and that is the single most important forward risk on this page. The second question was Australian, and it went the other way. TradingEconomics has capitulated: its calendar for Monday's RBA now carries consensus 4.60% and a TEForecast of 4.60% against 4.35% previous, where twenty-four hours ago it still said hold. The canonical source and the 92-94% market price now agree, all four major banks forecast the hike, trimmed mean inflation is stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band and Q2 GDP came in above expectations. AUD goes to +2. The third question - the yen - reopened rather than resolved. USD/JPY fell 1.02% to 157.252, giving back the 158.30 break this page flagged as unanswered, and the reason is that 160 is now an explicit line: Finance Minister Katayama said the principles behind the joint US-Japan intervention of July 31 are still alive, Japanese authorities checked rates with dealers before the weekend, and macro funds cut leveraged short-yen carry into that risk. JPY goes from -1 to 0 on a failed break, not on a policy change - the BoJ is still at 1.25% with TE carrying an explicit 1.25% hold for October 30, and Tokyo CPI on October 1 is the next real trigger. The dollar, meanwhile, ended its best run since May: DXY 101.035, down 0.25%, though still up 0.81% on the week and 1.89% on the month. The crack is where this page said it would be, and it is no longer subtle. Final September University of Michigan sentiment printed 48.1, a four-month low, with the expectations index down 10.1% to 46.3 from 51.5, year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6% - the highest since June - and five-year at 3.4%. Durable goods held flat at $338.6bn while core capital goods rose 1.6%, so business investment is fine and the household is not. That is a stagflationary mix, October pricing sat still at roughly 67.5% rather than extending, and the US 10-year eased to 5.17 with the 10-year TIPS real yield at 2.84%. USD comes off +3 to +2 - still the strongest currency here, but on growth and term premium rather than on an accelerating Fed. Europe took the clearest hit. German GfK consumer climate for October collapsed to -30.6 against -27.4 expected from a revised -26.8, with income expectations falling from +1.7 to -15.0 and willingness to save rising from 15.5 to 21.5, explicitly blamed on energy costs. That is the growth leg of the hawkish-ECB trade breaking on the same day the inflation leg got cheaper crude, with the October 29 decision close to a coin flip, so EUR drops from +1 to 0. New Zealand quietly changed shape too: TE's calendar now carries October 28 as a hold at 2.75% with the hike to 3.00% sitting at December 9, reversing the October emphasis this page carried yesterday, and NZD is the worst currency on the month at -4.76%. The franc is the cleanest expression of de-escalation and it keeps losing: USD/CHF 0.82827, up 2.83% on the month, an SNB at zero with symmetric intervention wording and 0.8% inflation, so CHF goes to -1. Metals confirm the same regime from the other side - gold 4285.00 and silver 64.259 finished higher on the day but down 2.25% and 2.99% on the week, because a 2.84% real yield is a punitive carry and de-escalation removes the premium that was offsetting it. The cleanest trades are therefore the ones that do not need a view on oil at all: AUD/NZD long on two hiking central banks with different calendars, AUD/CAD long on a three-point gap where the commodity split itself favours Australia because copper is physically tight while crude falls, and USD/CAD long, where yesterday's risk leg has flipped into a tailwind.

today.headline: USD/JPY fell 1.02% to 157.252 as the 158.30 break failed and 160 turned into an explicit official line rather than a psychological one
today.read: UP from -1 to 0, and the reason to read this entry is that the page's own call was wrong within a day - the break this page described as unanswered got answered. Finance Minister Katayama said the principles behind the joint US-Japan intervention of July 31 are still alive, Japanese authorities checked rates with dealers in overseas markets before the weekend, and macro and systematic desks cut leveraged short-yen carry into that tail risk rather than wait to find out. Iran diplomacy took some dollar off the top at the same time, which is why the move came with the rest of the board quiet. What has NOT changed is policy: the BoJ is at 1.25% after September 18, TE carries an explicit 1.25% hold for October 30, and board member Masu said only that hikes continue with the pace hinging on the July baseline and on crude, AI demand and FX. So this is a positioning repair inside a weak-currency story, not a turn - which is why JPY goes to 0 rather than positive, and why XXX/JPY longs move to lower conviction rather than flipping. Forward, the trigger is Tokyo CPI on October 1: headline is 1.9% with core 1.7%, and a soft print makes a second 2026 hike hard to argue. The second-round effect of Hormuz cuts the same way, because cheaper imported energy is exactly what removes BoJ urgency. Practical read: 160 is defended, 157 is the carry floor, and this is a range to trade rather than a trend to chase.

today.headline: TradingEconomics abandoned its 4.35% hold forecast and now carries both consensus and its own call at 4.60% for Monday's RBA, matching 92-94% market pricing
today.read: UP to +2, and this is the cleanest upgrade on the page because the evidence that changed is the canonical source itself. For a week this page flagged an open conflict - TE said hold, the market said 92-94% hike - and named it the only event where the priced outcome and the canonical forecast openly disagreed. That conflict is gone: TE's calendar for September 29 at 04:30Z now shows Previous 4.35%, consensus 4.60% and TEForecast 4.60%. All four major Australian banks forecast the hike. The case is the sturdiest here: trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band with the decline stalled, headline 3.5%, quarterly 3.9% y/y, Q2 GDP above expectations, August employment +39,493 after -15,864, and only unemployment at 4.6% from 4.5% pointing the other way. Crucially, none of that depends on the oil price, which makes AUD the one hawkish currency on this board that survives Hormuz reopening intact - and it is why AUD/NZD and AUD/CAD are the two cleanest tickets today. Forward, the risk inverts after Monday: at 92-94% priced the hike itself is not the trade, the guidance is, and a hike delivered with a cautious statement is a textbook sell-the-fact into an AUD/USD that is already down 1.38% on the week. Copper helps the second leg - physically tight, with LME available metal at 133,725 tonnes and cash at a $26 premium to three-month having swung from an $86 discount a week ago.

today.headline: The best dollar run since May ended with DXY down 0.25% to 101.035, and the consumer crack this page named as the invalidation finally fired
today.read: DOWN from +3 to +2, and the downgrade is about the composition of the data rather than the level. Final September University of Michigan sentiment came in at 48.1, a four-month low, with the expectations index down 10.1% to 46.3 from 51.5, current conditions 50.9 from 51.9, year-ahead inflation expectations up to 4.6% - the highest since June - and five-year at 3.4%. Set against durable goods orders flat at $338.6bn with core capital goods up 1.6%, the picture is business investment holding while the household deteriorates and its inflation expectations rise. That is a stagflationary mix and it is precisely the trigger this page named after the labour-crack trigger failed. Note what did not happen: October pricing sat still at roughly 67.5% rather than extending, the 10-year eased to 5.17, and the 10-year TIPS real yield is 2.84%. So the dollar remains the strongest currency here - the Fed is at 4.00% after a unanimous September 16 hike, composite PMI 58.4 is the strongest since July 2021, DXY is up 0.81% on the week and 1.89% on the month - but it is being paid for growth and term premium, not for an accelerating central bank, and the September SEP has the dots stopping at one more hike and then holding for a year. Forward: FOMC minutes October 7, then October 28. Invalidation is now a genuine consumption print rolling over, not another sentiment survey.

today.headline: German GfK consumer climate for October collapsed to -30.6 against -27.4 expected, with income expectations falling from +1.7 to -15.0 on energy costs
today.read: DOWN from +1 to 0, and it is the growth leg of the thesis that broke rather than the policy leg. The GfK detail is worse than the headline: income expectations went from +1.7 to -15.0, their weakest since April, and willingness to save rose from 15.5 to 21.5, with the survey attributing both directly to high energy prices cutting household purchasing power. That landed on the same Friday that Brent fell 2.14% - so the inflation argument for the ECB got cheaper at the same moment the growth argument got worse, which is the specific combination that makes a hawkish ECB hard to hold. The policy position itself is unchanged and still firm: the deposit facility rate is 2.50% after the September 10 hike, with the main refi at 2.65%. But reported pricing for October 29 is openly contradictory - 58% for a hike to 2.75% on one read, 61% for no change on another - and TE attaches no forward forecast, so this is a coin flip rather than a priced tightening. Underneath, euro-area inflation of 3.2% with core at 2.4% is mostly a fuel story: negotiated wage growth is 2.44% and falling, broad wage growth 3.0% from 3.4%. GDP rebounded to 1.2% y/y and unemployment is 6.4%. Forward, the hawkish case needs energy to stay expensive, and Friday said it may not. EUR/AUD goes short and EUR/USD stays short.

today.headline: Sterling firmed 0.22% to 1.32478 after Bailey ratified his deputies, but the barrel his hawkishness is explicitly conditioned on fell 2.14% the same day
today.read: HOLDS +1, with the tag changed rather than the score, because the risk to this position moved from the Governor to the oil price. Bailey said on Friday at the Oxford / New York Fed / Bank of England conference that the Bank has not increased Bank Rate and that it is 'going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices', adding that the Bank cannot wait for the full evidence of energy feeding into inflation expectations while describing that evidence as 'quite subdued'. Read literally, that is a conditional hawkish commitment - and the condition weakened within hours. No other central bank on this board has tied its turn to energy so explicitly, which makes sterling the most Hormuz-sensitive hawkish currency here and is the reason GBP does not go to +2 on a 75%-priced November. The rest is unchanged: Bank Rate 3.75% on a 6-3 vote, with Lombardelli and Breeden having moved out of the hold majority on the same conditional logic, against a composite PMI of 51.7, inflation 3.1% with core 2.6%, unemployment 4.9%, employment change +67k from +83k and wage growth cooling to 3.9% from 4.2%. Spot is up 0.22% on the day but down 1.10% on the week and still within a cent of a three-month low. Forward, the October 28 Budget with borrowing 8.1bn above the OBR profile is the bigger of the two UK events, and a sustained fall in Brent is the cleanest invalidation.

today.headline: Crude fell 2.33% and took the one remaining argument for the Bank of Canada with it, leaving USD/CAD at 1.41421 and up 1.11% on the week
today.read: HOLDS -1 and stays the weakest currency here, with the difference from yesterday being that the risk to being short CAD has turned into a tailwind. Twenty-four hours ago Brent at 106.60 sat five dollars above the US$100 level Macklem's hawkish conditional was written against, and this page flagged that as the leg working against USD/CAD longs. Brent is now 104.320 and falling on Hormuz reopening talks, which pushes that conditional back out of reach and weakens Canada's terms of trade at the same time. Everything domestic still points the same way: the overnight rate frozen at 2.25% since well before September 2, a 175bp discount to the Fed, August employment -41.7k after +75.1k, the only contracting PMIs on this board at 46.8 services and 47.8 composite, and July core retail sales down 0.7% against -0.5% expected with volumes down 1.1%. The counterweights are real but thin: Q2 GDP rebounded to 1.1% y/y and 3.3% annualized off a weak base, inflation is 3.0% with core ticking up to 2.4%, and producer prices at 12.4% keep a cut off the table - so this is a frozen central bank, not an easing one. Forward, the October 19 Business Outlook Survey is the only catalyst before October 28. AUD/CAD and USD/CAD are the cleanest expressions.

today.headline: No New Zealand data and NZD/USD unchanged at 0.56620, but TE's calendar quietly moved the next hike from October 28 to December 9
today.read: HOLDS 0, with the path reshaped rather than the score. TE now carries October 28 at 01:00Z with Previous 2.75% and a TEForecast of 2.75% - an explicit hold - while December 9 carries a TEForecast of 3.0%, which reverses the October emphasis this page ran yesterday. That matches Assistant Governor Silk pointing to December rather than October and the RBNZ's own OCR track. Reported market pricing genuinely contradicts itself here - one read has at least 75% for 3% on October 28, another has 88% for no change - and since that cannot be resolved from the available sources, TE's hold call is what this page carries and the disagreement is being stated rather than hidden. Governor Breman's warning that near-term inflation could overshoot if higher crude persists was the basis for the October case, and crude fell 2.33% on Friday, so that argument is weaker than it was. The underlying data stays the most conflicted on the board: inflation 4.1% is the highest of these eight economies and rising from 3.1%, while unemployment climbs to 5.6% from 5.4%, wage growth is only 2.1% and GDP rebounded to 2.6% y/y. NZD is the worst currency on the month at -4.76%, which is what a steep priced path meeting a weak economy looks like. AUD/NZD long is the cleanest way to hold this view.

today.headline: USD/CHF barely moved at 0.82827 but is up 2.83% on the month, and reopening talks remove the last argument for owning francs
today.read: DOWN to -1, and the downgrade follows the regime rather than any Swiss data. The SNB's September 24 assessment, verified in full at snb.ch, is effectively a standing instruction: the policy rate is 0.00% for a third consecutive assessment, the conditional inflation forecast assumes 0% across the entire horizon to 2029, and June's stated 'increased willingness to intervene' against rapid and excessive appreciation has been replaced with symmetric standby wording. Schlegel put the franc's trade-weighted depreciation since June at around 3% and called it in line with widening rate differentials - offered as explanation, not complaint - and TE's own wrap read the day as the SNB pushing back against intervention. The conditional inflation forecast was marked up at every horizon to 0.7/0.8/0.8 for 2026-2028, with the medium-term markup attributed partly to the franc's own weakness, which is a central bank telling you it is content. Against that, the economy is genuinely solid: GDP 2.3% y/y, unemployment 3.0%, employment up 0.5%. It does not matter for the currency while inflation is 0.8% and the rate is zero. Hormuz reopening talks take out the haven premium that was the only remaining bid, so CHF crosses go long against every currency with a live central bank.

strength.tag: Still the widest yield, but the consumer trigger finally fired

strength.forward: 🦅 Hawkish into October 28 but down a notch, and the reason is composition. The labour-crack invalidation this page named failed outright a day ago with claims at a two-month low; the consumer invalidation has now fired properly, with sentiment at 48.1 and the expectations sub-index down 10.1% in a month while inflation expectations rose to 4.6%. Deteriorating households with rising price expectations is the one mix that gives an inflation-targeting committee no clean answer, which is exactly why October pricing sat still at roughly 67.5% through Friday instead of extending on strong PMIs. The structural cap is unchanged and it is the real constraint: the September 16 SEP has the median funds rate at 4.1% for both 2026 and 2027, so the dots stop at one more hike and then hold for a year, and TE's own model projects 4.25% in 2027 and 4.00% in 2028. Falling crude helps here rather than hurting - it takes pressure off the inflation side without touching the growth side, which is a soft-landing input, not a dollar-negative one. Invalidation: a real consumption or payrolls print rolling over, or October pricing breaking below about 50% into the FOMC minutes on October 7.

strength.tag: The most hawkish words on the board, tied to the one price that fell
strength.drivers: Bank Rate 3.75%, held September 17 on a 6-3 vote. Bailey on Friday: the Bank has not increased Bank Rate and it is 'going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices', and it cannot wait for the full evidence of energy feeding into inflation expectations - which he called 'quite subdued'. Lombardelli and Breeden both moved out of the hold majority on the same conditional logic, taking reported November 5 pricing to roughly 75%. Against that: composite PMI 51.7, inflation 3.1% with core 2.6%, unemployment 4.9%, employment change +67k from +83k, wage growth cooling to 3.9% from 4.2%, gilt 10-year near 5.38 and an October 28 Budget with borrowing 8.1bn above the OBR profile. strength.forward: ⚖️ Hawkish in word, conditional in substance, and Friday made the condition the trade. Bailey has now committed the MPC in public to a hawkish lean that he himself framed as a function of energy prices staying high - and within hours of him saying it, Brent fell 2.14% on Hormuz reopening talks. No other central bank here has made its turn so explicitly contingent on a single price, which makes sterling the most de-escalation-sensitive of the hawkish currencies and is precisely why GBP stays at +1 with a MIXED verdict rather than being marked up on 75% November pricing. Two counterweights sit underneath: he called the evidence on inflation expectations 'quite subdued' in the same breath, and the market barely responded to the ratification. Forward, the order of events matters - the October 28 Budget comes eight days before the November 5 meeting, and with borrowing already 8.1bn above profile a fiscal loosening would do more to gilts and sterling than the MPC will. Hold sterling long against the franc, the Canadian dollar and the New Zealand dollar; do not hold it against the Australian dollar into Monday. Invalidation: Brent sustained below about US$95, or a Budget that widens the deficit.

strength.tag: 160 got defended and the break gave a big figure back

Finance Minister Katayama said the principles behind the joint US-Japan intervention of July 31 are still alive; Japanese authorities checked rates with dealers in overseas markets before the weekend, historically a precursor to action; macro and systematic desks unwound leveraged short-yen carry into that risk. Board member Masu said the Bank will keep raising the policy rate with the pace hinging on the July baseline and on crude, AI-driven demand and FX. Headline CPI 1.9% with core 1.7%, wage growth 4.7% from 4.0%, unemployment 2.4%, GDP 0.7% y/y. Tokyo CPI is due October 1.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Range rather than direction, and the upgrade from -1 to 0 is a correction this page owes: the 158.30 break it described as unanswered was answered inside a day, and by the Ministry of Finance rather than by the data. What that establishes is a defended ceiling. 160 is now an explicit official line backed by a live precedent in the July 31 joint intervention, rate checks before the weekend and a finance minister repeating that those principles hold - so the tail risk of chasing yen shorts through 158 is now larger than the carry earned for doing it. Nothing underneath has turned. The BoJ is at 1.25% with TE showing an explicit October 30 hold, the differential to the Fed is still roughly 275bp, and cheaper crude cuts imported inflation and therefore cuts the Bank's urgency - a quiet second-round effect of Hormuz that argues against a December move. Tokyo CPI on October 1 is the decider: headline 1.9%, core 1.7%, and a soft print makes a second 2026 hike hard to argue. Trade 157-160 as a range, keep XXX/JPY longs at lower conviction, and note that a genuine intervention would be a one-off shock rather than a trend change. Invalidation: an actual intervention, or a firm Tokyo CPI reviving December.

Invalidation: core CPI re-accelerating above 2.6%, or German gas spiking again. Short EUR/USD and EUR/AUD, long EUR/CAD and EUR/CHF.

Forward, the October 28 statement is now about the OCR track rather than the rate, and Q3 CPI in mid-October is the print that matters more. Invalidation either way: a surprise October hike, or unemployment above 5.8%. Express this short against AUD and GBP, not against the dollar alone.

catalysts.event: RBA cash rate decision and statement - Reserve Bank of Australia
catalysts.note: THE event of the coming week, and it is marked med rather than high only because ForexFactory's next-week red-folder feed returns 404 from this environment, so the time below is taken from TE's calendar rather than from FF. Treat it as the highest-impact release on this page. TE now carries Previous 4.35%, consensus 4.60% and a TEForecast of 4.60%, having shown a 4.35% hold as recently as yesterday - the capitulation that removed the only open conflict between the canonical source and market pricing at 92-94%. All four major Australian banks forecast the hike. The case: trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band with the decline stalled, headline 3.5%, quarterly 3.9% y/y, Q2 GDP above expectations, August employment +39,493. A hike takes Australia to the highest policy rate of the majors, 60bp above the Fed's upper bound and 210bp above the ECB deposit rate. Because it is 92-94% priced, the tradeable content is the statement and any guidance on whether 4.60% is terminal, not the rate itself.

catalysts.event: BoE Governor Bailey speaks - Bank of England
catalysts.note: DELIVERED, and he ratified rather than pushed back. On the policy panel at the sixth Oxford / New York Fed / Bank of England monetary economics conference at St Hilda's College, alongside Lucrezia Reichlin and the New York Fed's John Williams, Bailey said the Bank has not increased Bank Rate and that it is 'going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices', adding that the Bank cannot afford to wait for the full evidence on how high energy prices are feeding into inflation expectations - while describing that evidence so far as 'quite subdued'. No new forecasts, no vote and no published speech text accompanied the remarks. The reason this entry still matters twenty-four hours later is the conditional: Brent fell 2.14% the same day on Hormuz reopening talks, which means the Governor has publicly tied the MPC's hawkish lean to a price that is now falling. Context: Lombardelli and Breeden, both inside the 6-3 majority that held Bank Rate at 3.75% on September 17, had each signalled that persistent energy prices may force a hike, taking November 5 pricing to roughly 75%. Market response was muted - GBP/USD 1.32478, +0.22% on the day and still within a cent of a three-month low.

catalysts.event: SNB press conference - Swiss National Bank
catalysts.note: HELD, and the introductory remarks are verified in full at snb.ch. Schlegel put the franc's trade-weighted depreciation since June at around 3% and called it 'in line with the widening of interest rate differentials between the major currency areas and Switzerland', noting Swiss long rates have not risen as strongly as elsewhere - an explanation offered without objection. Petra Tschudin credited 'our monetary policy and the recent depreciation of the Swiss franc' with supporting growth guided up to 1.5-2% for 2026, and Antoine Martin observed that key rates were raised in both the euro area and the US. TE's own European wrap summarised the day as the SNB having held as expected and pushed back against franc intervention. The SNB publishes no Q&A transcript and no vote split - decisions are taken by consensus among a three-member Governing Board - so nothing beyond the prepared text is verifiable. The franc has kept weakening since, with USD/CHF at 0.82827 and +2.83% on the month, and CHF moves to -1 today as Hormuz de-escalation removes the last haven argument.

catalysts.event: SNB monetary policy assessment and policy rate - Swiss National Bank
catalysts.note: RELEASED, verified at snb.ch and on TradingEconomics: the policy rate held at 0.00% for a third consecutive assessment, in line with consensus and TE's own forecast, with the discount on sight deposits above the threshold unchanged at 0.25 percentage points. The rate was never the event. The conditional inflation forecast was marked UP at every horizon to 0.7% for 2026, 0.8% for 2027 and 0.8% for 2028, against June's 0.6/0.6/0.7, with the near-term markup attributed to higher-than-expected prices for oil products and the medium-term markup to, among other things, the weakening of the Swiss franc - and the forecast assumes a 0% policy rate across the entire horizon to 2029. The FX clause changed: June's 'increased willingness to intervene' against a rapid and excessive appreciation was replaced by symmetric standby wording. Growth is guided to 1.5-2% for 2026 and around 1.5% for 2027, with the Middle East named as the main risk - a risk that de-escalated this week, which cuts against the franc rather than for it.

catalysts.note: DELIVERED and it did not derail Monday. Employment rose 39,493 in August after -15,864 in July, while the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.6% from 4.5%. catalysts.note: The single most important input on this page and the reason six of eight currency entries changed today, which is why it is carried at high impact despite having no scheduled time. The reason to treat this as two-way rather than directional: the same channel produced a June 17 memorandum of understanding that collapsed into renewed fighting within weeks, and the IEA still describes the traffic restriction through the strait as the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market. Four central banks - the BoE, the ECB, the RBNZ and to a lesser degree the BoC - have hawkish cases that rest on high energy prices, so a durable reopening unwinds all four at once, while a collapse restores them.

geopolitics: The de-escalation trade this page abandoned on Thursday came back on Friday, and this time the tape agreed with it. Prices first, all from TradingEconomics. WTI is 92.410 and Brent 104.320, down 2.33% and 2.14% on the day, with WTI down 3.82% on the week; gasoline fell 4.80% to 3.3934 and European gas was down 3.06% at 3.1960 even while holding a 9.75% weekly gain. The trigger was diplomatic rather than physical: Iranian and US negotiators held side talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly about a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif used his UNGA address to publicise Islamabad's mediation between Washington and Tehran and to warn about the economic fallout of the conflict. TradingEconomics' own European equity wrap names the same cause, attributing the DAX's 0.5% gain to optimism around a potential agreement to reopen the strait. Two things have to be said about durability, because the position sizing depends on them. The first is that this exact channel has failed before within this same year: the June 17 memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran, which also promised safe passage, collapsed into renewed fighting, and the June and September pattern of talks-then-escalation is why a single session of headlines is not a regime. The second is that the underlying disruption has not been repaired - the IEA still characterises the restriction of traffic through the strait as the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, and Brent at 104.320 is still a war price, roughly fifty per cent above where it was a year ago. So the honest description is a risk premium being partially discounted, not removed. The FX transmission is where this gets genuinely tradeable, and it is asymmetric in a way that is easy to miss. Four of the eight central banks here have hawkish cases that were built explicitly on expensive energy. Bailey said on Friday it would 'get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices'. Lombardelli warned that persistent energy prices risk building indirect effects into inflation expectations and wage bargaining; Breeden used the tinderbox image. RBNZ Governor Breman warned near-term inflation could overshoot if higher crude persisted. The euro-area case is the same in substance - 3.2% headline against 2.4% core with negotiated wages at 2.44% and falling is a fuel story. Every one of those arguments weakens if Brent keeps falling, which means sterling, the euro and the New Zealand dollar all carry a hidden short-oil exposure inside their hawkish theses. The Australian dollar does not: trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6% with a Q2 GDP beat is a domestic problem, TE has now capitulated to a 4.60% hike on Monday, and that is the entire reason AUD is the currency to own into de-escalation rather than the dollar. On the other side, Canada is the clean loser - falling crude both weakens its terms of trade and puts Macklem's hawkish conditional, written against the US$100 level, back out of reach, which keeps CAD at the bottom of this board. The franc is the second loser and for the purest reason: strip out the haven premium and what remains is a zero policy rate the SNB assumes will hold until 2029, symmetric intervention wording, 0.8% inflation and a central bank that described a 3% trade-weighted depreciation as in line with rate differentials, so CHF goes to -1. Gold and silver confirm the same regime from the other direction - both rose on Friday but lost 2.25% and 2.99% on the week, because a 2.84% ten-year TIPS real yield is a punitive carry once the geopolitical premium starts to leak out. The invalidation for all of it is a single headline: talks breaking down, as they did after June 17, would put Brent back through US$110 and restore four hawkish central bank cases, a weak CAD short and a haven bid in one move. That is why USOIL is short at medium rather than high conviction, and why the trades this page prefers today - AUD/NZD, AUD/CAD, USD/CAD - are the ones whose primary driver is a central bank calendar rather than a barrel.
